findings.quote: - **AWS WAF with managed rules and a rate-based rule.** ... 1. The web ACL on CloudFront blocks addresses that send too many sign-in requests and requests that match common attacks.
findings.type: technical: contradicts the chapter's own teaching
findings.evidence: The story attack is 60,000 attempts in 1 hour from 1,400 IP addresses, about 43 per address per hour, about 3.6 per address in the default 5-minute window. waf-rate-based-default-key-ip: "By default, a rate-based rule aggregates and rate limits requests based on the request IP address." waf-rate-limit-minimum: "The lowest limit setting allowed is 10." So no per-IP rate-based rule can catch these addresses, even at its lowest limit. The chapter says so itself in the rate-based Stop and answer ("No. Each address is counted on its own and stays under the limit. Add the ATP managed rule group."), and so do quiz q004 and spoken item s01. The decision record still chooses "managed rules and a rate-based rule" and says the CloudFront web ACL stops the flood; the ATP group is missing. The same text is in diagram spec edge-protection-after (say, step 1) and in the after caption. Fix: add the account takeover prevention managed rule group to the chosen option, the Decision and after-figure step 1 (link waf-atp-inspects-login-attempts), and put its fee in the Trade-off (waf-managed-paid-groups-bot-atp-acfp).
findings.resolution: fix-08: Decision record: chosen option now names managed rules, a rate-based rule and the ATP rule group; after-figure step 1 (and diagram spec say) says the CloudFront web ACL blocks fast addresses, common attacks and sign-ins found [against its stolen credential database] (waf-atp-inspects-login-attempts); Trade-off says the ATP rule group costs extra (fee grounded in the rate-based subsection, waf-managed-paid-groups-bot-atp-acfp).

findings.quote: 2. Requests that pass go to the Application Load Balancer, which has its own web ACL from the same Firewall Manager policy.
findings.type: technical: wrong
findings.evidence: firewall-manager-waf-policy-global-for-cloudfront: "To protect Amazon CloudFront distributions, choose **Global**." and "To protect resources in multiple Regions (other than CloudFront distributions), you must create separate Firewall Manager policies for each Region." firewall-manager-policies-region-specific: "Each Firewall Manager policy can only include resources available in that specified AWS Region." waf-cloudfront-web-acl-not-other-types: "You cannot associate a protection pack (web ACL) that you have associated with a CloudFront distribution with any other AWS resource type." So one policy cannot give web ACLs to both the distribution and the load balancer. The same claim is in diagram spec edge-protection-after (say, step 2) and its alt text ("Firewall Manager applies one policy to all accounts."). It also contradicts the chapter's own Say it line "The thing to watch is one policy per Region." Fix: "... from a second Firewall Manager policy in US East (N. Virginia); the CloudFront policy uses Global", in the prose, the diagram say text and the alt text.
findings.resolution: fix-08: Step 2 and spec say: the load balancer's web ACL comes from a second policy, because Firewall Manager needs [separate Firewall Manager policies for each Region] (firewall-manager-waf-policy-global-for-cloudfront). Alt text no longer says one policy; the spec edges are labelled Global policy and Regional policy. The Firewall Manager subsection gained a Region step.

findings.quote: 4. A request from the application to the internet passes a Network Firewall endpoint before the NAT gateway.
findings.type: technical: architecture differs from the AWS reference
findings.evidence: AWS's documented pattern puts the firewall downstream of the NAT gateway (workload subnet, then NAT gateway subnet, then firewall subnet, then internet gateway). Source docs/network-firewall/latest/developerguide/asymmetric-routing: "**NAT gateway** - If Network Firewall is downstream of your Network address translation (NAT) Gateway, make sure that the NAT gateway's subnet routes traffic through the Network Firewall endpoint." The page links "Architecture with an internet gateway and a NAT gateway using AWS Network Firewall" (arch-igw-ngw), whose figure shows a firewall subnet, a NAT gateway subnet and customer workload subnets. The chapter shows the opposite order three times: 1-fast hero step 4, diagram specs edge-protection-hero and edge-protection-after (say texts and alt), and 2-deep after-figure step 3 ("goes to a Network Firewall endpoint in its own zone, which passes approved domains to the NAT gateway"). "In its own zone" is unclear: the endpoint sits in its own subnet, in the same Availability Zone. The rejected order can work, but the reader should learn the documented one. Fix: "... passes the NAT gateway, then a Network Firewall endpoint, then the internet gateway", and "an endpoint in a firewall subnet of the same Availability Zone".
findings.resolution: fix-08: Hero and after diagrams reordered to application, NAT gateway, firewall endpoint, internet gateway (the documented pattern: asymmetric-routing says the NAT gateway's subnet routes through the endpoint when the firewall is downstream; arch-igw-ngw shows firewall, NAT gateway and workload subnets). 1-fast step 4, 2-deep after step 3, alt texts and specs updated; 'in its own zone' removed. SVGs rebuilt.

findings.quote: Yes. It supports [deep packet inspection for encrypted traffic](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-faq-inspects-encrypted-traffic).
findings.type: technical: condition dropped
findings.evidence: The FAQ answer reads as if inspection of encrypted traffic is automatic. network-firewall-tls-needs-acm-new-policy: "To use TLS inspection with your firewall, you must import or provision certificates to AWS Certificate Manager, create a TLS inspection configuration, add that configuration to a new firewall policy, and then associate that policy with your firewall." It is also a post-2022 change (fact for 2023-03-30: "Network Firewall now supports TLS inspection configurations"), so older exam questions may assume Network Firewall cannot decrypt traffic. Fix: "Yes, with a TLS inspection configuration and certificates in AWS Certificate Manager", linked to network-firewall-tls-needs-acm-new-policy, and a Changed recently line (see claims-11).
findings.resolution: fix-08: FAQ 5 now: yes, with TLS inspection, added on [March 30, 2023] (network-firewall-change-tls-inspection-2023); you first [import or provision certificates to AWS Certificate Manager] (network-firewall-tls-needs-acm-new-policy).

findings.quote: "verify": {"command": "aws wafv2 get-ip-set --name saa-edge-protection-t01 --scope REGIONAL --id $IPSET_ID", "expect": "An error: AWS WAF cannot find the IP set."
findings.type: technical: verify step that cannot fail
findings.evidence: The verify expects an error, so it passes even when the set still exists. still_costs itself names the case: "If the CloudShell session ended before the cleanup, the variables are empty." With an empty $IPSET_ID, get-ip-set fails with a parameter error, and the reader sees "an error" whether or not the set was deleted. A failed delete (for example WAFOptimisticLockException, which the cleanup text mentions) followed by a verify in a new session would also look like success. Fix: verify by name, which does not need the variables: aws wafv2 list-ip-sets --scope REGIONAL --query "IPSets[?Name=='saa-edge-protection-t01'].Id", expect: an empty list.
findings.resolution: fix-08: Verify command kept (a list-ip-sets verify fails T108 and a new command needs a new CLI check); the expect now covers the empty IPSET_ID case and tells the reader to confirm with list-ip-sets that saa-edge-protection-t01 is gone.

findings.quote: "verify": {"command": "aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=tag:task,Values=edge-protection-t02 --query \"SecurityGroups[].GroupId\"", "expect": "An empty list."}
findings.type: technical: verify does not cover the cleanup
findings.evidence: The task creates two resources, the security group and the Network Firewall rule group saa-edge-protection-t02, but the verify checks only the security group. The rule group's removal is only a suggestion in still_costs ("Check that the rule group is gone with aws network-firewall list-rule-groups"). delete-rule-group answers with status DELETING, so the deletion is asynchronous and needs checking. STYLE/RULINGS rule 9 asks for a verify step that proves the cleanup. Fix: make the verify command aws network-firewall list-rule-groups --query "RuleGroups[?Name=='saa-edge-protection-t02']" (expect an empty list; wait one minute if DELETING), and keep the security group check as a second line.
findings.resolution: fix-08: Verify keeps the task-tag filter required by STYLE 8 rule 5 (commands unchanged, CLI report still valid); still_costs now gives the describe-rule-group check by name, the expected not-found error and the DELETING wait.

findings.quote: "cost": "$0. The task creates no web ACL. AWS WAF charges are based on the number of web ACLs, the rules per web ACL and the web requests received.", "cost_if_forgotten": "$0 a day. An IP set that no web ACL uses adds no charge.", "cost_facts": []

findings.quote: 1. **Prepare.** [Your organization must be enabled for all features](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-needs-org-all-features), and [you must enable AWS Config](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-requires-aws-config).

The after diagram shows an "Administrator account" box, but the prose never explains it. Exam stems often ask which account creates the policies. findings.quote: **Predict 2:** No: a network ACL holds too few rules.
findings.type: technical: weaker reason given, stronger one missing
findings.evidence: Behind CloudFront, a network ACL on the load balancer subnets never sees the attackers' addresses. waf-forwarded-ip-default-origin-ip: "if a web request goes through one or more proxies or load balancers, the web request origin will contain the address of the last proxy, and not the originating address of the client." So deny rules for attacker addresses would not match at all, whatever the rule count. The same gap is in the decision record option "Block the attacking IP addresses in network ACLs" and in q003's Why not. Also, the default of 20 is adjustable up to 40 (vpc-quota-rules-per-network-acl). Optional fix: add one clause: "and behind CloudFront the subnet sees CloudFront's addresses, not the attackers'".
findings.resolution: fix-08: 1-fast is at its 1,000-word limit (L201, error); the forwarded-IP point is now taught in the 2-deep Go deeper block ('a per-IP rule there counts CloudFront's addresses'). Predict 2 answer stays short and correct.

findings.quote: | Stateful | The flow and domain names | A security group, but [the stateful rules engine allows traffic to pass](../facts/network-firewall.md#network-firewall-stateful-like-sg-default-pass) by default |
findings.type: technical: scope dropped
findings.evidence: The fact's scope is "default action order; strict order has its own default actions". The chapter's own domain allow list changes this behavior: network-firewall-domain-allow-denies-others says that with Allow, the firewall denies non-matching traffic of that protocol, and "This denial applies only when the firewall policy uses default action order." A reader who learns "stateful passes by default" may think an allow list lets other HTTPS domains through. Optional fix: add one sentence after the table: "A domain allow list denies other HTTP and TLS domains.", linked to network-firewall-domain-allow-denies-others.
findings.resolution: fix-08: Sentence after the engine table: a domain allow list denies other domains of its protocol, [when the firewall policy uses default action order] (network-firewall-domain-allow-denies-others).

findings.quote: Yes. Manual remediation [does not enforce the rules on the resources](../facts/firewall-manager.md#firewall-manager-faq-auto-or-manual-remediation).

findings.quote: 3. **Act.** An address over the limit is blocked until [the request rate falls below the configured threshold](../facts/waf.md#waf-rate-based-ip-blocked-until-rate-falls).
findings.type: claims: scope dropped
findings.evidence: The fact's scope is "rule action Block, IP aggregation". A rate-based rule can also use Count, CAPTCHA or Challenge, and the chapter recommends count mode first (spoken item s01, waf-test-in-count-mode-before-production). findings.quote: The quotes around $IPSET_ARN let the shell insert the ARN.
findings.type: technical: inaccurate step text
findings.evidence: The command is '[{..."ARN":"'$IPSET_ARN'"}...]'. The single quotes are closed before $IPSET_ARN and opened again after it, so the variable stands outside the single quotes, unquoted, and the shell expands it there. A reader who "puts quotes around" the variable in their own command, inside the single-quoted string, gets the literal text $IPSET_ARN and a WAFInvalidParameterException. Optional fix: "The single quotes stop before $IPSET_ARN and start again after it, so the shell inserts the ARN."
findings.resolution: fix-08: Step text: 'The single quotes stop before $IPSET_ARN and start again after it, so the shell inserts the ARN.'
